items.readable_text:
Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to negate statements involving universal and existential quantifiers.

Content:
To negate the universally quantified statement
[MATH: \forall x \in U, \, P(x)]
we flip the quantifier to existential and negate the predicate:
[MATH: \neg \left( {\color{blue}\forall} x \in U, \, {\color{red}P(x)} \right) \equiv {\color{blue}\exists} x \in U, \, \neg {\color{red}P(x)}]

Content:
To see why it makes sense to do this, let's negate the following statement:

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] All integers are even.

Content:
This statement can be re-phrased as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] For all [MATH: n \in \mathbb{Z},] [MATH: \left(2 \mid n\right).]

Content:
Introducing the universal quantifier, we get the following:

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: \forall n \in \mathbb{Z}, \, \left(2 \mid n \right)]

Content:
Negating this according to the above rule, we obtain

Content:
[MATH: ¬(∀n ∈ Z, (2∣n))|≡∃n ∈ Z, ¬(2∣n); ≡∃n ∈ Z, (2∤n).]

Content:
This statement now reads

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] There exists [MATH: n \in \mathbb{Z}] such that [MATH: n] is not even.

Content:
We can write this in more everyday English in the following ways:

Content:
- There is at least one odd integer.
- Some integers are odd.

Content:
This makes intuitive sense. The statement that "all integers are even" is false, and the reason it's false is that at least one integer is odd.

To negate the existentially quantified statement

we flip the quantifier to universal and negate the predicate:

Content:

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] There is a real number whose square is negative.

Content:
The given statement can be re-phrased as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] There exists [MATH: x \in \mathbb{R},\, x^2 < 0.]

Content:
Introducing the existential quantifier, we get the following:

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: \exists x \in \mathbb{R},\, x^2 < 0.]

Content:
This statement is false, and so its negation must be true.

Content:
Negating this according to the above rule, we obtain

Content:
[MATH: ¬(∃x ∈ R, x^{2} < 0)|≡∀x ∈ R, ¬(x^{2} < 0); ≡∀x ∈ R, x^{2} ≥ 0.]

Content:

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] For all [MATH: x \in \mathbb{R},] [MATH: x^2\geq 0].

Content:
We can write this in more everyday English as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] The square of every real number is nonnegative.

Content:

sections.normalized_html:
Negate the following statement:

[MATH: \qquad] Some quadrilaterals are squares.
sections.readable_text:
Negate the following statement:

[MATH: \qquad] Some quadrilaterals are squares.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let [MATH: Q] be the set of all quadrilaterals and [MATH: S] the set of all squares. The given statement can be re-phrased as follows:

[MATH: \qquad] There exists [MATH: q \in Q] such that [MATH: q \in S]

Introducing the existential quantifier, we get the following:

[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: \exists q \in Q, \, q \in S.]

Negating this, we obtain [MATH: ¬(∃q ∈ Q, q ∈ S)|≡∀q ∈ Q, ¬(q ∈ S); ≡∀q ∈ Q, q ∉ S]

which reads

[MATH: \qquad] For all [MATH: q \in Q,] [MATH: q \not\in S.]

or simply

[MATH: \qquad] All quadrilaterals are not squares.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to negate statements involving universal and existential quantifiers.

Content:

[MATH: \forall x \in U, \, P(x)]

[MATH: \neg \left( {\color{blue}\forall} x \in U, \, {\color{red}P(x)} \right) \equiv {\color{blue}\exists} x \in U, \, \neg {\color{red}P(x)}]

Content:
To see why it makes sense to do this, let's negate the following statement:

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] All integers are even.

Content:
This statement can be re-phrased as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] For all [MATH: n \in \mathbb{Z},] [MATH: \left(2 \mid n\right).]

Content:

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: \forall n \in \mathbb{Z}, \, \left(2 \mid n \right)]

Content:

Content:
[MATH: ¬(∀n ∈ Z, (2∣n))|≡∃n ∈ Z, ¬(2∣n); ≡∃n ∈ Z, (2∤n).]

Content:
This statement now reads

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] There exists [MATH: n \in \mathbb{Z}] such that [MATH: n] is not even.

Content:
We can write this in more everyday English in the following ways:

Content:
- There is at least one odd integer.
- Some integers are odd.

Content:
This makes intuitive sense. The statement that "all integers are even" is false, and the reason it's false is that at least one integer is odd.
